{{Short description|German chemist and medical physicist (born 1951)}}
[[File:Jürgen Hennig.jpg|thumb|240px|Jürgen Hennig (2010)]]
'''Jürgen Klaus Hennig''' (born in [[Stuttgart]], [[Germany]] on March 5, 1951) is a German [[chemist]] and medical physicist. Internationally he is considered to be one of the pioneers of [[Magnetic Resonance Imaging]] for clinical diagnostics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zeitung |first=Badische |date=2014-08-02 |title=Der Forscher Jürgen Hennig ist der Meister der Kernspins |url=https://www.badische-zeitung.de/der-forscher-juergen-hennig-ist-der-meister-der-kernspins |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=Badische Zeitung |language=de}}</ref> He was until his retirement 2022 the Scientific Director of the Department of Diagnostic Radiology and Chairman of the Magnetic Resonance Development and Application Center (MRDAC) at the [[University Medical Center Freiburg]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Innovation in MRI: Back to the Future? |url=https://www.tuebingen.mpg.de/217730/plenary-speakers |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=www.tuebingen.mpg.de |language=en}}</ref> Despite his retirement, he is still active as a researcher (as of 3/2025). In In addition to numerous scientific awards he received in 2025 the [[Order of Merit of Baden-Württemberg|Order of Merit of the state Baden-Wuerttemberg.]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Max Planck Research Awards 2003 |url=https://www.mpg.de/481878/max-planck-research-awards-2003 |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=www.mpg.de |language=en}}</ref> He is married to Annemarie Hennig Rüegg and has two children, Julian and Olivia. Olivia died in 2009.

== Biography ==

=== Scientific career ===
From 1969 to 1977 Hennig studied chemistry in [[Stuttgart]], [[London]], [[Munich]] and [[Freiburg]]. During the years from 1977 to 1981 he was employed as a scientist at the [[Institute of Physical Chemistry of the Polish Academy of Sciences|Institute of Physical Chemistry]] (IPC) of the [[University of Freiburg]], where he completed his doctoral degree on NMR measurements of intramolecular exchange kinetics under the supervision of Herbert Zimmermann.<ref>{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|title=Physikalisch-chemische Untersuchungen des Vibrationstunneleffektes bei der intramolekularen Wasserstoffwanderung in Tetraarylporphinen |location=Freiburg|date=  1980|language=German}}</ref> During this time Hennig first came into contact with [[Magnetic Resonance Imaging]] (MRI) at the inaugural lecture of his advisor Hans-Heinrich Limbach on the work of [[Paul Lauterbur]], a subsequent winner of the [[Nobel Prize]].<ref name="china">{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|periodical=Encyclopedia of Magnetic Resonance|title=How RARE Came to China: Early Days of MRI |date=  2010|language=German|doi=10.1002/9780470034590.emrhp1025}}</ref>

From 1982 to 1983 Hennig was a post-doctoral student at the [[University of Zurich]], where he worked in the area of [[CIDNP]] Spectroscopy. In 1982 he developed his first own [[NMR]] [[pulse sequence]] to measure intramolecular exchange processes.<ref>{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|surname2=H. H. Limbach|periodical=J Magn Reson|title=Magnetization transfer in the rotating frame: A new simple kinetic tool for the determination of rate constants in the slow chemical exchange range |volume=49|issue=2|pages=322–328|date=  1982|language=German|doi=10.1016/0022-2364(82)90195-0|bibcode=1982JMagR..49..322H}}</ref> During his time in Zurich Hennig decided to focus his future work in the area of NMR method development with less focus on chemistry.<ref name="china" />

Hennig began his work at the [[University Medical Center Freiburg]] in 1984 as a scientific researcher in the Department of Diagnostic Radiology. There, in cooperation with the company [[Bruker|Bruker Medizintechnik GmbH]], he developed the RARE-Method.<ref name="RARE">{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|surname2=A. Nauerth|surname3=H. Friedburg|periodical=Magn Reson Med|title=RARE imaging: A fast imaging method for clinical MR |volume=3|issue=6|pages=823–833|date=  1986|language=German|doi=10.1002/mrm.1910030602|pmid=3821461|s2cid=25261837}}</ref> In the year 1989 he completed his professorial thesis of “Special Imaging Techniques for the Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Tomography” at the Medical Faculty of the [[University of Freiburg]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Qian |first=JC |title=Professor Juergen Hennig visits High Magnetic Field Laboratory |url=http://english.hmfl.cas.cn/ne/ns/202202/t20220225_248237.html |website=the chinese academy of sciences}}</ref>

In the year 1993, Hennig was appointed a professorship at the [[University Medical Center Freiburg]] as the head of the MR Tomography work group in the Department of Diagnostic Radiology.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2019-07-29 |title=Jürgen Hennig |url=https://www.neuromod.uni-freiburg.de/people/jurgen-hennig/ |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=NeuroModulBasics |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1998 he was designated as the Director of the Department of Imaging and Functional Medical Physics of the Department of Diagnostic Radiology. In 2001 he became Research Director of the Department of Diagnostic Radiology. In the same year he founded the Magnetic Resonance Development and Application Center (MRDAC) at the University Medical Center Freiburg. A cooptation at the School of Mathematics and Physics of the [[University of Freiburg]] followed in the year 2002.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ultra-fast brain imaging to become even more precise |url=https://www.uniklinik-freiburg.de/en/press/focal-points/medical-technology/detailed-view/707-ultraschnelle-bildgebung-fuers-gehirn-soll-noch-praeziser-werden.html |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=www.uniklinik-freiburg.de |language=en}}</ref>

In 2004 Hennig was appointed C4-[[Professor]] at the [[University Medical Center Freiburg]] and since then he is the Scientific Director of the Department of Diagnostic Radiology. The research group for research and development in MRI that he founded and headed since 1984 grew to approximately 80 employees by the end of 2012.<ref name=":0" />

In 1999 Hennig was the President of the [[International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine]] (ISMRM). 
Since 2008 he has been a joint affiliate to the Wisconsin Institute for Medical Research at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].
Since 2011 he has been a member of the [[German Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]].<ref name=":2" />

=== Works ===
Hennig’s research work was aimed at fundamental, preclinical, clinical research as well as clinical applications. His main areas of research were [[neurology]] and [[neuroscience]], [[oncology]], [[Heart|cardiac]] and [[Circulatory system|cardiovascular]], and [[Metabolism|metabolic research]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=TechTalk – Innovation in MRI: Back to the Future? – Innovation Wing |url=https://innowings.engg.hku.hk/innovation-in-mri/ |access-date=2026-04-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> His goal was to give space for free and fundamental research, but once a new method turned out to be clinically useful, he went all the way to bring it to clinical application.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Kiviniemi |first2=Vesa |last3=Riemenschneider |first3=Bruno |last4=Barghoorn |first4=Antonia |last5=Akin |first5=Burak |last6=Wang |first6=Fei |last7=LeVan |first7=Pierre |date=2021-02-01 |title=15 Years MR-encephalography |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10334-020-00891-z |journal=Magnetic Resonance Materials in Physics, Biology and Medicine |language=en |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=85–108 |doi=10.1007/s10334-020-00891-z |issn=1352-8661|pmc=7910380 }}</ref> He always found it important to be open to different application scenarios rather than being focused on one specific application domain. More than once he found out, that a method first developed for a specific area of application (like cardiac) has turned out more useful in another area (like neuroscience).Hennig has written numerous fundamental research papers on the development of [[Magnetic Resonance Imaging]] (MRI).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |date=2023 |title=An evolution of low-field strength MRI |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37289275 |journal=Magma (New York, N.Y.) |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=335–346 |doi=10.1007/s10334-023-01104-z |issn=1352-8661 |pmc=10386941 |pmid=37289275}}</ref>

Based on the CPMG multi-echo method, Hennig developed the RARE Sequence (Rapid Acquisition with Relaxation Enhancement) in 1984.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fast / Rapid Imaging • Magnetic Resonance in Medicine – The Basics – by Peter A. Rinck {{!}} NMR MR MRI {{!}} Essentials, introduction, basic principles, facts, history {{!}} The primer of EMRF/TRTF. |url=https://www.magnetic-resonance.org/ch/08-02.html |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=www.magnetic-resonance.org}}</ref> Through his work the MR image acquisition time could be significantly reduced, which constituted an important step for its use in clinical routine.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Barghoorn |first2=Antonia |last3=Zhang |first3=Shuoyue |last4=Zaitsev |first4=Maxim |date=2022 |title=Single shot spiral TSE with annulated segmentation |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.29224 |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |language=en |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=651–662 |doi=10.1002/mrm.29224 |issn=0740-3194|doi-access=free |arxiv=2111.14914 }}</ref> In addition, RARE offered the possibility to control the diagnostically relevant T2 contrast in MRI. The RARE method was first published in 1984 in the German journal “Der Radiologe”.<ref>{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|surname2=A. Nauerth|surname3=H. Friedburg|surname4=D. Ratzel|periodical=Radiologe|title=Ein neues Schnellbildverfahren für die Kernspintomographie |volume=24|pages=579–580|date=  1984|language=German}}</ref> His first submission to an international journal was rejected, with the comment that this method had already been tested and wouldn’t work.<ref name="china" /> In the year 1986 international publications followed.<ref name="RARE" /><ref>{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|surname2=H. Friedburg|surname3=B. Strobel|periodical=J Comput Assist Tomogr|title=Rapid nontomographic approach to MR myelography without contrast agents |volume=10|issue=3|pages=375–378|date=  1986|language=German}}</ref> RARE is currently one of the standard methods used in clinical [[MRI]]. The method is also known by the acronyms TSE (Turbo Spin Echo) and FSE (Fast Spin Echo).

In 1991 Hennig published the so-called [[Extended phase graph|Extended Phase Graph]](EPG)-method, which allows to calculate the signal intensity after MR-sequences with an arbitrary number of radiofrequency pulses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=J |date=1988-07-01 |title=Multiecho imaging sequences with low refocusing flip angles |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/002223648890128X |journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance  |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=397–407 |doi=10.1016/0022-2364(88)90128-X |issn=0022-2364|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The EPG method is intensely used in the design of many current MR-methods like MR-Fingerprinting.<ref name="Hennig 2021 85–108">{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Kiviniemi |first2=Vesa |last3=Riemenschneider |first3=Bruno |last4=Barghoorn |first4=Antonia |last5=Akin |first5=Burak |last6=Wang |first6=Fei |last7=LeVan |first7=Pierre |date=2021 |title=15 Years MR-encephalography |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33079327 |journal=Magma (New York, N.Y.) |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=85–108 |doi=10.1007/s10334-020-00891-z |issn=1352-8661 |pmc=7910380 |pmid=33079327}}</ref> It has also been the basis of the development of the Hyperecho and  and TRAPS-methods, which were published by Hennig in 2001<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Scheffler |first2=Klaus |date=2001 |title=Hyperechoes |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.1153 |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |language=en |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=6–12 |doi=10.1002/mrm.1153 |issn=0740-3194}}</ref> and 2003 respectively. These allow to significantly reduce the [[specific absorption rate]] (SAR) of a RARE sequence without loss of image quality, which is essential for clinical [[MRI]] applications at high [[magnetic field]] strengths of 3T and higher.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Weigel |first2=Matthias |last3=Scheffler |first3=Klaus |date=2004 |title=Calculation of flip angles for echo trains with predefined amplitudes with the extended phase graph (EPG)-algorithm: principles and applications to hyperecho and TRAPS sequences |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14705047 |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=68–80 |doi=10.1002/mrm.10658 |issn=0740-3194 |pmid=14705047}}</ref>

In 2008 Hennig published a concept for imaging with [[Magnetic field|non-linear magnetic field]] [[gradient]]s which allows to use stronger and faster magnetic field gradients.<ref>{{citation|surname1=J. Hennig|surname2=A. Welz|surname3=G. Schultz|surname4=J. Korvink|surname5=Z. Liu|surname6=O. Speck|surname7=M. Zaitsev|periodical=Magn Reson Mater Phy|title=Parallel imaging in non-bijective, curvilinear magnetic field gradients: a concept study |volume=21|pages=5–14|date=  2008|issue=1–2|language=German|doi=10.1007/s10334-008-0105-7|pmid=18299913|pmc=2798019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.esmrmb.org/cms/website.php?id=/en/lectures_on_mr/lectures_on_mr_courses_2015/inverse_imaging_sparse_sampling_compressed_sensing_and_more_.htm&template=print |title=.: ESMRMB - Online :.: Inverse imaging, sparse sampling, compressed sensing, and more |website=www.esmrmb.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151004180925/http://www.esmrmb.org/cms/website.php?id=/en/lectures_on_mr/lectures_on_mr_courses_2015/inverse_imaging_sparse_sampling_compressed_sensing_and_more_.htm&template=print |archive-date=2015-10-04}}</ref>

This development was performed in the context of the bi-national innovation project INUMAC/ISEULT, in which Hennig coordinated the German academic research effort.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hammerschmidt |first=Christoph |date=2006-11-24 |title=Medical imaging funded by France, Germany |url=https://www.edn.com/medical-imaging-funded-by-france-germany/ |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=EDN |language=en-US}}</ref>

As a radical new approach to increase imaging speed Hennig developed in 2005 the MR-encephalography(MREG)-method, which in its ultimate form does not require any magnetic field gradients for spatial encoding but uses the sensitive volumes of multiarray receiver-coils as primary source of spatial information. In the current standard implementation some gradient encoding is used to increase [[spatial resolution]], while still maintaining an unprecedented imaging speed of 10 volumes per second for a whole brain 3D-dataset with 3&nbsp;mm isotropic resolution. The method has been distributed to many research groups worldwide and is used to observe dynami variations in brain network activities as well as for investigation of the glymphatic system of the brain.<ref name="Hennig 2021 85–108"/>

In the mid-2010s Hennig advocated the concept of a 5T-whole body MRI scanner as a practical field strength for whole body MRI.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Jürgen |date=1993 |title=Overlapping section coverage in multisection imaging |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.1880030219 |journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging |language=en |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=425–432 |doi=10.1002/jmri.1880030219 |issn=1053-1807|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 7T-scanners were already on the market, but there use was focused on brain imaging and they had to be typically placed outside of the radiological suite due to their large size.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Evolution of Field Strength in MR: Back to the Future? |url=https://www.tic-sitem.ch/blog/the-evolution-of-field-strength-in-mr-back-to-the-future |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=The Evolution of Field Strength in MR:  Back to the Future? |language=en}}</ref>

Whole-body imaging at 7T was limited by the high radiofrequency power at that field strength, which does not allow to use the full diagnostic repertoire of methods common at lower field strength.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Juergen |last2=Welz |first2=Anna Masako |last3=Schultz |first3=Gerrit |last4=Korvink |first4=Jan |last5=Liu |first5=Zhenyu |last6=Speck |first6=Oliver |last7=Zaitsev |first7=Maxim |date=2008 |title=Parallel imaging in non-bijective, curvilinear magnetic field gradients: a concept study |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2798019/ |journal=Magma (New York, N.Y.) |volume=21 |issue=1-2 |pages=5–14 |doi=10.1007/s10334-008-0105-7 |issn=0968-5243 |pmc=2798019 |pmid=18299913}}</ref> Hennig hypothesized,  that a 5T system would allow the full use of diagnostic examination methods and would be small enough to fit into a typical examination room.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hennig |first=Jürgen |date=2025 |title=Quo Vadis MRI? |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11910256/ |journal=Zeitschrift für Medizinische Physik |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=3–5 |doi=10.1016/j.zemedi.2024.12.002 |issn=1876-4436 |pmc=11910256 |pmid=39800646}}</ref> He propagated the idea on several conferences and in discussion with various vendours. In 2016 he could convince United Imaging of the concept. The final product was launched in 2024, the performance confirmed and exceeded the expectations and earned Hennig the title ‘Father of 5T’.<ref name=":4" />

In 2022 Hennig combined his RARE-method with spatial encoding using a segmented spiral k-space trajectory. This allows to acquire a high-resolution image with 1&nbsp;mm spatial resolution in ~ 200 ms. This SpiralTSE-method can be used for fast parametric imaging and allows to quantify multi-exponential T1- and T2- parameters, as well as magnetic transfer(MT) effects in well under 3 min.<ref name=":5" />

=== Connections to Asia ===
In the year 1985 Hennig travelled to [[Guangzhou]], China in order to set up one of the first [[MRI]] systems in China. With this the first MR image was taken in China on December 25, 1985.  Since then he has attended other MRI system installations in China.<ref name="china" />

Hennig has been president and founding member of the European-Chinese Society for Clinical Magnetic Resonance since 1993.<ref name=":2" /> He is honorary member of the [[Chinese Radiological Society]]. Hennig was awarded “Einstein Professor” of the Chinese Academy of Science in 2011. In 2010 he received the [[:de:Tsungming-Tu-Preis|Tsung Ming Tu Award]], which is the highest scientific award of [[Taiwan]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=German scientist awarded Taiwan's top academic prize |url=https://taiwantoday.tw/AMP/society/top-news/17574/german-scientist-awarded-taiwan%E2%80%99s-top-academic-prize |website=Taiwan Today}}</ref>

Since 2004 Hennig is a member of the Academy of Science of the Republic of [[Tatarstan]]. Furthermore, he maintains cooperations with Hong Kong, South Korea and Singapore.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-11-17 |title=Hounsfield Memorial Lecture 2015: Magnetic Resonance Imaging: Visions of Life {{!}} Imperial News |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/169171/hounsfield-memorial-lecture-2015-magnetic-resonance/ |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=Imperial College London |language=en-GB}}</ref>

=== Statistics ===
His group had a total 286 members since 1993, he supervised 94 PhD Thesis.<ref name=":4" />

Until his retirement in December 2021, he had published 515 publications in peer reviewed scientific journals with a total number of 998 co-authors, 50 as first author and 119 as last author. His top 3 journals are: ''[[Magnetic Resonance in Medicine]]'' (116) ''[[Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging]]'' (27) and ''Magnetic Resonance Materials in Physics Biology and Medicine'' (25).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Google Scholar |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Qh2Le2sAAAAJ&hl=en#:~:text=D%20H%C3%A4ussinger,%20J%20Laubenberger,%20S,,%20W%20Greffrath,%20... |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

== Awards ==
* 1992: ''European Magnetic Resonance Award''<ref name="emra">[http://magnetic-resonance.org/ch/20-10.html Award winner list of the European Magnetic Resonance Award]</ref> 
* 1993: 'Kernspintomographie-Preis' (Magnetic Resonance Tomography Award) 1993
* 1994: Gold Medal Award of the Society of Magnetic Resonance<ref name="ismrm">[http://www.ismrm.org/about/society-award-winners/ Gold Medal Award winner list International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine]</ref>

* 2010: [[:zh:杜聰明獎|Tsung Ming Tu Award]] from the National Science Council, Taiwan<ref name=":3" />
* 2014: Honorary Doctorate from the [[Maastricht University|University Maastricht]]<ref name=":1" />
* 2015: Hounsfield Memorial Lecture [[Imperial College London]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Hounsfield Memorial Lecture|trans-title=|website=www.hounsfieldlecture.org|publisher=|url=http://www.hounsfieldlecture.org/|format=|access-date=2016-07-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160721141002/http://www.hounsfieldlecture.org/|archive-date=2016-07-21|last=|date=|year=|language=German|pages=|quote=|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2016: [http://www.drg.de/de-DE/29/alfred-breit-preis Alfred-Breit-Preis from Deutschen Röntgengesellschaft (German radiological Society)]<ref>{{cite web|title=Alfred-Breit-Preis {{!}} DRG.de|trans-title=|website=www.drg.de|publisher=|url=http://www.drg.de/de-DE/29/alfred-breit-preis|format=|access-date=2016-07-21|last=|date=|year=|language=German|pages=|quote=}}</ref>
